core.text: To say what someone is trying to achieve, Latin adds **ut / ne + subjunctive (the 'in order to' clause: venit ut videat = comes to see)**: *ut* (so that) for an aim, *nē* (so that … not) for something to avoid. Its verb is in the subjunctive (the form Latin uses for wishes, purposes and what someone tells someone to do). Latin name: *coniūnctīvus fīnālis*.
English: he came *to see* her; she hid *so that no one would find* her. Purpose is the aim, not what happened.
ut / nē + present subjunctive after a present main verb, imperfect subjunctive after a past one. The negative is nē, never ut nōn.

invented.la: Servus ad urbem currit ut medicum vocet.
invented.en: The slave runs to the city to call a doctor.
The girl kept quiet so that her mother would not hear.

core.text: A result clause also uses *ut*, but after a signal word — *tam* (so), *ita* (in such a way), *tantus* (so big) — and its negative is *ut nōn*. Aim = purpose; outcome = result: *tam stultus est ut crēdat*, so foolish that he believes.
After a verb of ordering or asking (*imperat* orders, *rogat* asks), *ut* + subjunctive is the order itself: *imperat ut solvat*, orders him to pay — an indirect command, not a purpose.

more.text: A relative word can carry the purpose: *quī* + subjunctive = 'someone to …', *quō* + subjunctive = 'so that by it': *nāvis parārētur quā Ulixēs redīre posset* — a ship was to be got ready in which he could sail home (Week 5). Translate as if the relative were *ut*.

The learner's notes put it this way: a purpose clause states the intent of an action — *veniunt ad mēnsam ut cēnent* (they come to the table to dine), *moritur ut vīvāmus* (he dies so that we may live); the relative kind (*veniunt quī cēnent*) is best translated without the relative. Ørberg's chapter 29 pairs the tenses: *Dāvus clāmat ut puerum excitet* / *clāmāvit ut puerum excitāret*.

Other ways Latin says 'in order to': *ad* + gerund (*ad nāvigandum*, for sailing), the supine after a verb of motion (*spectātum veniunt*, they come to watch), *causā* with a genitive gerund. With a comparative, *quō* replaces *ut*: *quō facilius* … = so that … more easily.

teach.title: Saying why
teach.say: To say what an action is for, Latin adds a clause: **ut / nē + subjunctive (the 'in order to' clause: venit ut videat = comes to see)**. *Servus ad urbem currit ut medicum vocet* — the slave runs to the city in order to call a doctor. The clause names the aim and nothing more: whether the doctor is ever called, the sentence does not say.

teach.title: Why the infinitive will not do
teach.say: English says 'comes to look'. Latin cannot: it has no 'to' of purpose, so it writes *ut* with a subjunctive (the form Latin uses for wishes, purposes and what someone tells someone to do) — *venit ut spectet*. Never *venit spectāre*. When you are turning English into Latin, an English 'to' that means 'in order to' is your signal to write *ut* and change the verb.

check.ask: Fill the blank with the form of legō that ut needs here.

teach.title: nē for an aim to avoid
teach.say: For something the doer is trying to prevent, **nē** replaces *ut*: *tacet nē māter audiat*, 'she keeps quiet so that her mother will not hear'. A purpose clause has no *ut nōn*. The *nē* clause may also come first — *nē aeger fīat, aquam pūram bibit* — and the rule does not change with the word order.

check.ask: Fill the blank with the form of intrō that nē needs here.

teach.title: Not a result clause
teach.say: A result clause uses *ut* too, but it always answers a signal word — *tam* (so), *ita* (in such a way), *tantus* (so great), *tālis* (of such a kind) — and its negative is *ut nōn*. A purpose has no signal word and takes *nē*. The plainest test is to try 'in order' in the English: *runs in order to arrive first* works, so that is purpose; *so fast that nobody sees him* does not, so that is result.

check.ask: What is veniat here — the aim, or what came of it?

teach.title: Not an indirect command
teach.say: After a verb of telling (*imperat, ōrat, monet*) the *ut* clause is the order itself: **ut / nē + subjunctive (the form for what someone asks or orders someone to do)**. After any other verb — *mittit*, *dat*, *currit*, *īmus* — the same *ut* gives the aim. So look at the verb in front of the clause, not at the clause.

teach.title: quī can do the same work
teach.say: A relative word can carry the aim instead of *ut*: *mittit servum quī epistulam ferat*, 'he sends a slave to carry the letter'. It is the subjunctive *ferat* that marks it — a plain description would have the indicative (the plain fact form) *fert*, 'who is carrying the letter'. Read it as though *quī* were *ut is*: 'a slave to carry it'.
